Do this immediately:

1) Shut off water to the toilet
- Look behind or beside the toilet for a small metal valve on the wall/floor.
- Turn it clockwise (to the right) all the way until it stops. It may be stiff—use both hands if needed.
- If there is no valve or it won’t turn, find the **main water shutoff**:
  - House: often in the garage, utility room, or outside near the street under a metal/plastic cover.
  - Turn that valve clockwise until it stops. This will cut water to the whole place.

2) Stop the toilet refilling
- Take off the **tank lid** (back part of toilet).
- Inside:
  - Push the **rubber flapper** at the bottom closed with your hand.
  - Or lift the **float** (ball or cup) up and keep it up; this tells the tank to stop filling.
- That should stop water from continuing to come into the bowl.

3) Contain the water
- Unplug anything on the bathroom floor.
- Use towels to block the doorway and soak up water so it doesn’t reach other rooms.
- If water is going to a lower floor or toward outlets, and you can safely do it, switch off power to that area at the breaker.

Next: call an **emergency plumber in Austin** directly (since my system can’t finish a booking for your address right now).
Search on your phone for:  
“emergency plumber Austin 78701”  

When they answer, say:
- “My toilet is overflowing and water won’t stop. I’m at **123 Tech Park Drive, Austin, TX 78701**. I’ve shut off (or tried to shut off) the water. I need the fastest available plumber.”

If you tell me:
- Whether you found and turned the shutoff, and  
- What you see inside the tank (flapper, chain, float),  

I can walk you through a quick temporary fix while you wait for the plumber.</action>

<action type="say">
Good—that’s progress.

Here’s what to do next inside the tank:

1) Make sure new water can’t come in
- Keep the **float** (the thing on the pole) in the **up** position.  
  - If it wants to drop back down, gently bend the metal arm (if it’s metal) **down a bit where it meets the valve** so that, when the float is up, the water stays off.  
  - If the arm is plastic and can’t be bent, you can temporarily:
    - Wedge something under the float (like a plastic spoon, stick, or rolled-up plastic) to keep it **propped up**, or
    - Tie the float up to something solid with string, floss, or a twist-tie.

2) Seal the rubber flapper
- Press the **rubber flapper** at the bottom firmly down so it sits flat over the hole.
- Check the **chain**:
  - It should have a **little slack** when the flapper is down.
  - If it’s pulled tight, unhook it from the flush handle arm and move it to a **closer hole** so it’s looser, or just let it hang looser for now so the flapper can fully close.

3) CAREFUL test
- Very briefly, turn the **shutoff valve behind the toilet** a tiny bit **counterclockwise** (open) and watch:
  - If water starts rushing again into the bowl or overflowing, turn it **back clockwise all the way** immediately.
  - If water stays off and nothing is rising in the bowl, you’ve got it stable. Turn it back off fully until a plumber arrives so no one flushes by accident.

Important:
- Don’t use this toilet until a plumber has checked it.
- You still should call an emergency plumber and say:
  “Toilet overflowed badly, I shut off the valve and propped the float/flapper. I’m at 123 Tech Park Drive, Austin, TX 78701. I need someone ASAP to fix the toilet and check for any damage.”

Tell me:
- When you crack the valve back open a little, does the water stay off in the bowl, or does it start filling/rising again?</action>
